posts.body_html: Entirely possible that you are right Mike! Someone with his thinking cap on might be wondering why in sweltering Florida the plants were just opening during the second week in May! The burns were done late at these sites and the flava / leuco flower buds were all lost. This caused the plants to delay pitcher production until about a month past normal, perhaps as a protective mechanism against late frosts damaging the pitchers. To see these plants in this state I think the second week of April would be more biologically normal in that climate. Bud loss could have caused stress that affected color as well. BUT smaller plants that didn't flower this spring were not disrupted in the same way and had put out pitchers sooner. These had had more time to infuse and were more typical "atro" in appearance even next to plants that were not yet there color-wise. Doesn't disprove your theory though Mike since perhaps it was the loss of flower buds and not fire that could cause less initial color. Again, these were smaller seedling plants that didn't bloom, not mature clumps. No way to know if these smaller plants were solid red when they opened a couple weeks before we got there, but the positive relationship between age and color makes me think they were not. Damn! Guess we will just have to head back out there and do more research! A couple shots taken May 9:

posts.body_html: In cultivation and as a generalization, if you cut off all the dead winter traps from S. flava var. rubricorpora Liberty Co, FL (we won't talk about the mysterious bay co plants for now, LOL), the new traps tend to come out greenish (although some clones are so damn red that they'll still come up red).  Keep everything on from the previous year until you get new traps in the spring, and they'll start off as red as can be.

posts.body_html:
Forgot I had these shots meizzwang! Most of the plants didn't seem to be producing pitchers at all when we were there in late June but here and there fresh traps were emerging. Among those managed to spot a few red plants popping out new traps. Was excited to get these shots because they pretty much ruled out stress from fire or bud loss as a factor influencing early-season color (or young pitcher color, to put it more precisely), which were questions that Trey and I both wanted to resolve. They really do open ornata-y and suffuse over time. I am sure there are plants that are red before opening somewhere in these populations (like Liberty Co red tubes, whose bodies are often red pre-opening), but we did not see them on this trip. I think there is actually a lot more going on with "atropurpurea" genetics than I ever appreciated before. They certainly aren't just "red plant, end of story" - will cook up a post on that soon!

Great pix Calen! Hard to say what can and can't be ruled out:as you mentioned, there seems to be a whole lot more going on than what meets the eye. Those look very moorei or leucophylla influed to me, especially with the ruffles in the hood.

For sure, them solid red flavas in that area are quite diverse! I wonder if start out solid red is an "exception to the rule" in this area much like the Bay Co, FL rubricorporas? Would be interesting to see and compare multiple solid red black water populations opening up in the spring when there is no fire.

posts.body_html:
Ahahaha not the "that atro is a hybrid" gag again!  Yep likely some leuco in there at some point - sheesh I doubt there is a single flava in any of those crazy cray diverse sites that doesn't have leuco and / or rosea in it somewhere. You are totally right however Mike - those pics are circumstantial evidence and don't rule anything out necessarily. We are just going to have to go back to those sites this coming spring and see what the plants look like without a burn.

Since meizzwang brought up the moorei question, let me drop some rank speculation! Based on what we saw, my guess would be that originally the red flavas begot the red mooreis, and not the other way around. Seemed like there generally had to be red flavas nearby to find red mooreis - bogs with leucos and green flavas had green mooreis. Just a hunch but I'd put money on the red color coming from rosea via x naczii, stabilizing in the flava population, and then being passed on to moorei clones. Of course, once formed the red mooreis could re-inject red genes into green flavas, possibly forming red flavas that do have a moorei as their most recent red ancestor. I suppose it's also possible that through some unknown mechanism a green flava crossing to a leuco could create red mooreis de-novo. For example the throat blotch on mooreis is often bigger than on the rugelii parent - the throat blotch gene was "amplified" somehow when the plants were crossed. And many of philcula's best red mooreis come from his (leuco Purple Lips x flava ornata) crosses, and neither of those plants is particularly "red." So truth be told there might be more than one path to a red flava, but if I had to theorize on what mostly/probably happens / the primary mechanism, rubles to ribeyes it was the rosea genes, not the leuco genes. 

Not really adding anything new, but I just found these excellent shots taken by Julie Tew one week after Trey and I visited this same site (May 15 vs. May 9). The red flavas have already colored up further, but still aren't all the way there.
